title: An uncountable almost-disjoint family of infinite coordinate subsets
statement: There exist an uncountable set $I$ (one admitting no injection into $\mathbf N$, equivalently one for which $\operatorname{Countable}(I)$ fails in the sense of [def-sfb-countable-set]) and subsets $A_i\subseteq\mathbf N$ for $i\in I$ such that each $A_i$ is infinite and $A_i\cap A_j$ is finite whenever $i\ne j$ [def-sfb-finite-infinite-set].

proof.text: Take $I=\mathcal P(\mathbf N)$. By [lem-sfb-cantor-no-powerset-injection] with $X=\mathbf N$, no function $I\to\mathbf N$ is injective. Thus $I$ is uncountable with exactly the meaning of [def-sfb-countable-set].

source.place: Paragraph (3), combinatorial auxiliary; explicit binary-prefix proof written by NF, not asserted by the blueprint paragraph.

proof.text: Encode finite words in the digits $\{0,1\}$ by $c([])=1$ and $c(b::w)=2c(w)+b$, where $b::w$ is the word with head $b$ and tail $w$. All codes are positive by induction. The code is injective: induct on the sum of the lengths of two words with equal codes. An empty word cannot have the same code as a nonempty word, whose code is at least $2$. For two nonempty words, reduction modulo $2$ gives equal heads, and subtraction and division by $2$ give equal tail codes; the induction hypothesis gives equal tails. This proves equality of the words.

source.place: Paragraph (3), combinatorial auxiliary; explicit binary-prefix proof written by NF, not asserted by the blueprint paragraph.

proof.text: For $S\in I$, define its digit $s(k)$ to be $1$ if $k\in S$ and $0$ otherwise. Let $w_S(n)=[s(0),\ldots,s(n-1)]$, including $w_S(0)=[]$, and put $A_S=\{c(w_S(n)):n\in\mathbf N\}\subseteq\mathbf N$. Equality $c(w_S(n))=c(w_T(m))$ implies equality of the two words by step 2, hence $n=m$ and $s(k)=t(k)$ for every $k<n$.

source.place: Paragraph (3), combinatorial auxiliary; explicit binary-prefix proof written by NF, not asserted by the blueprint paragraph.

proof.text: For each $S$, the function $n\mapsto c(w_S(n))$ is injective by the equality-of-lengths conclusion of step 3. If $A_S$ were finite, of size $r$, its elements $c(w_S(0)),\ldots,c(w_S(r))$ would be $r+1$ distinct members of a set of size $r$, a contradiction. Therefore each $A_S$ is infinite in the sense of [def-sfb-finite-infinite-set].

source.place: Paragraph (3), combinatorial auxiliary; explicit binary-prefix proof written by NF, not asserted by the blueprint paragraph.

proof.text: Let $S\ne T$ in $I$. Choose $k\in\mathbf N$ at which their membership digits differ; such a $k$ exists by extensionality of subsets. If $a\in A_S\cap A_T$, write $a=c(w_S(n))=c(w_T(m))$. Step 3 gives $n=m$. If $k<n$, equality of the words gives $s(k)=t(k)$, contradicting the choice of $k$. Thus $n\le k$, so $A_S\cap A_T\subseteq\{c(w_S(0)),\ldots,c(w_S(k))\}$. The right side has at most $k+1$ elements, and hence the intersection is finite as in [def-sfb-finite-infinite-set]. Together with steps 1 and 4 this gives every clause of the statement.
